name: Cardiomyopathies
tagline: Primary diseases of the myocardium itself — dilated, hypertrophic, restrictive and arrhythmogenic — many of them genetic and familial.
overview: Cardiomyopathies are diseases in which the myocardium is structurally and functionally abnormal in the absence of coronary disease, hypertension, valve disease or congenital disease sufficient to explain it. The traditional morphological classification remains useful: dilated cardiomyopathy with ventricular enlargement and impaired systolic function; hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with inappropriate hypertrophy, usually from sarcomeric protein mutations; restrictive cardiomyopathy with impaired filling and preserved wall thickness in the early stages; and arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy with fibrofatty replacement, classically of the right ventricle. Many are inherited, so identifying one has implications for the whole family.

modifiable: Cardiotoxic chemotherapy, especially anthracyclines and trastuzumab
nonModifiable: Sarcomeric gene mutations in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Desmosomal gene mutations in arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy
Titin and lamin A/C variants in dilated cardiomyopathy
Family history of cardiomyopathy or sudden death
Amyloidosis, sarcoidosis and other infiltrative disease

pathophysiology.title: Dilated cardiomyopathy
pathophysiology.text: Myocyte injury, loss and disarray with interstitial fibrosis lead to eccentric remodelling. The ventricle dilates and becomes spherical, wall stress rises by Laplace's law, and systolic function progressively declines.

pathophysiology.title: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
pathophysiology.text: Sarcomeric protein mutations produce myocyte hypertrophy and disarray with interstitial fibrosis. Wall thickening is typically asymmetric and septal, impairing relaxation and reducing cavity size.

pathophysiology.title: Dynamic outflow obstruction
pathophysiology.text: In obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, septal hypertrophy narrows the outflow tract; rapid flow draws the anterior mitral leaflet into it (systolic anterior motion), causing dynamic obstruction and mitral regurgitation. The gradient increases with reduced preload or increased contractility.

pathophysiology.title: Restrictive cardiomyopathy
pathophysiology.text: Infiltration or fibrosis stiffens the myocardium. Ventricular volumes and systolic function are initially preserved but filling is severely impaired, producing marked atrial dilatation and high filling pressures.

pathophysiology.title: Arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy
pathophysiology.text: Desmosomal protein mutations weaken cell–cell adhesion. Myocytes are progressively replaced by fibrous and fatty tissue, creating a substrate for re-entrant ventricular arrhythmia, often exacerbated by exercise.

pathophysiology.title: Common downstream consequences
pathophysiology.text: Whatever the mechanism, the shared endpoints are heart failure, arrhythmia and thromboembolism, with sudden cardiac death a particular concern in hypertrophic and arrhythmogenic forms.

anatomyInvolved: Ventricular myocardium and its sarcomeres, desmosomes and interstitium
Interventricular septum, asymmetrically thickened in hypertrophic disease
Mitral valve apparatus, involved in systolic anterior motion
Atria, markedly dilated in restrictive disease
Right ventricular free wall in arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy
physiologyChanges: Reduced ejection fraction and stroke volume in dilated disease
Impaired relaxation with elevated filling pressures in hypertrophic and restrictive disease
Dynamic, load-dependent left ventricular outflow gradient in obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Reduced coronary flow reserve despite normal epicardial arteries
Increased arrhythmic substrate from fibrosis and myocyte disarray

progression.text: A pathogenic variant is present without detectable structural change. Requires longitudinal surveillance.
Early structural or functional abnormality detected on imaging without symptoms.
Breathlessness, chest pain, palpitations or syncope, with the pattern depending on the subtype.
Progressive heart failure, sustained arrhythmia, or the need for transplantation or mechanical support.

symptoms: Exertional breathlessness and fatigue
Chest pain, often without coronary disease
Palpitations and syncope, particularly exertional in hypertrophic and arrhythmogenic disease
Symptoms of right heart failure in restrictive disease
Sudden cardiac death as a first presentation, especially in young people
signs: Displaced apex with a third heart sound in dilated cardiomyopathy
Jerky carotid pulse, double apical impulse, fourth heart sound and an ejection systolic murmur that increases with Valsalva in obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Raised JVP with Kussmaul's sign in restrictive disease
Signs of systemic disease — macroglossia and periorbital purpura in amyloidosis
Frequently a normal examination in early disease

investigations.findings: Chamber dimensions, wall thickness and distribution, systolic and diastolic function, outflow gradient with provocation, and systolic anterior motion.
Accurate volumes and mass, and tissue characterisation — late gadolinium enhancement patterns, T1 and T2 mapping and extracellular volume — which often identify the aetiology.
Abnormal in most cases: voltage criteria, deep T-wave inversion, pathological Q waves, epsilon waves in ARVC, low voltage with pseudo-infarct pattern in amyloidosis.
Arrhythmia burden, blood pressure response to exercise, and functional capacity — all feeding into sudden death risk assessment.
Identifies the causative variant and enables cascade screening of first-degree relatives.
Reserved for suspected infiltrative or inflammatory disease; bone-tracer scintigraphy is highly useful in transthyretin cardiac amyloidosis.

complications: Sudden cardiac death from ventricular arrhythmia
Need for transplantation or mechanical circulatory support

treatment.principles: Treatment is directed by subtype and by arrhythmic risk. Dilated cardiomyopathy is managed with guideline-directed heart failure therapy. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy focuses on relieving obstruction and preventing sudden death. Restrictive disease requires treatment of the underlying infiltrative process. Family screening is part of the management of every inherited cardiomyopathy. Educational summary only.

groups.name: Heart failure therapy
groups.detail: Full guideline-directed medical therapy in dilated cardiomyopathy with reduced ejection fraction.

groups.name: Obstruction relief
groups.detail: Beta-blockers, disopyramide and cardiac myosin inhibitors; septal myectomy or alcohol septal ablation for refractory obstruction.

groups.name: Sudden death prevention
groups.detail: Risk stratification with validated tools, and implantable defibrillators for those at high risk.

groups.name: Arrhythmia management
groups.detail: Antiarrhythmic drugs, catheter ablation and, in arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy, exercise restriction.

groups.name: Disease-specific therapy
groups.detail: Transthyretin stabilisers and silencers in amyloidosis; immunosuppression in cardiac sarcoidosis; iron chelation in haemochromatosis.

groups.name: Family screening
groups.detail: Clinical and genetic evaluation of first-degree relatives, with longitudinal follow-up of gene carriers.

keyTakeaways: Cardiomyopathy is myocardial disease not explained by coronary, valve, hypertensive or congenital disease.
Four morphological patterns: dilated, hypertrophic, restrictive and arrhythmogenic.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the commonest inherited cardiac condition and a leading cause of sudden death in young athletes.
The outflow gradient in obstructive HCM is dynamic — it worsens with Valsalva, standing and hypovolaemia.
Cardiac MRI tissue characterisation frequently reveals the underlying aetiology.
Diagnosing a cardiomyopathy is diagnosing a family, not just a patient.

name: Congenital Heart Disease
tagline: Structural cardiac abnormality present from birth — the commonest congenital malformation, and now a lifelong adult specialty as survival has transformed.
overview: Congenital heart disease encompasses a wide range of structural abnormalities arising during cardiac development. It is the most common congenital malformation. Lesions are usefully grouped by their physiological consequence: left-to-right shunts, which cause pulmonary overcirculation and volume loading; obstructive lesions, which cause pressure loading; and cyanotic lesions, in which deoxygenated blood reaches the systemic circulation. Because surgical and interventional outcomes have improved so dramatically, most patients now survive to adulthood, and adult congenital heart disease has become a distinct specialty dealing with residual lesions, arrhythmia, heart failure and pregnancy.

modifiable: Maternal diabetes, particularly poorly controlled in the first trimester
Maternal rubella and other intrauterine infections
Maternal alcohol, lithium, retinoids, some antiepileptics and warfarin exposure
nonModifiable: Chromosomal abnormalities such as trisomy 21, 22q11 deletion and Turner syndrome
Single-gene disorders and family history of congenital heart disease

pathophysiology.title: Disrupted embryological development
pathophysiology.text: Abnormal septation, valve formation, outflow tract division or conotruncal rotation between roughly weeks three and eight of gestation produces the structural lesion.

pathophysiology.title: Transitional circulation
pathophysiology.text: At birth, pulmonary vascular resistance falls and systemic resistance rises. This reversal is what unmasks many left-to-right shunts, which may therefore present weeks after birth rather than immediately.

pathophysiology.title: Left-to-right shunting
pathophysiology.text: A communication between systemic and pulmonary circuits directs blood towards the lower-resistance pulmonary side, causing pulmonary overcirculation and volume loading of the receiving chambers.

pathophysiology.title: Obstructive physiology
pathophysiology.text: Stenotic lesions — pulmonary stenosis, aortic stenosis, coarctation — impose pressure loading, producing hypertrophy and, if severe, ventricular failure.

pathophysiology.title: Cyanotic physiology
pathophysiology.text: Right-to-left shunting or abnormal mixing allows deoxygenated blood into the systemic circulation, producing hypoxaemia, secondary erythrocytosis and clubbing.

pathophysiology.title: Eisenmenger physiology
pathophysiology.text: Long-standing high-flow left-to-right shunting causes pulmonary vascular remodelling and rising resistance until the shunt reverses, producing cyanosis and marking the point at which shunt closure is no longer possible.

anatomyInvolved: Atrial and ventricular septa
Cardiac valves, particularly pulmonary and aortic
Great arteries and their connections
Aortic arch and isthmus
Ductus arteriosus and foramen ovale
Pulmonary and systemic venous connections
physiologyChanges: Altered pulmonary-to-systemic flow ratio (Qp:Qs)
Volume or pressure loading of specific chambers according to the lesion
Progressive pulmonary vascular remodelling with sustained overcirculation
Hypoxaemia with compensatory erythrocytosis in cyanotic lesions
Long-term atrial and ventricular arrhythmia from surgical scar and chronic loading

progression.text: Detection on antenatal ultrasound, or presentation with cyanosis, murmur, shock or failure to thrive as the ductus closes.
Definitive repair or palliation for most significant lesions; some small defects close spontaneously.
Residual and recurrent lesions, valve regurgitation, conduit degeneration and arrhythmia.
Heart failure, atrial arrhythmia, pulmonary hypertension, and pregnancy and non-cardiac surgery risk requiring specialist management.

symptoms: Poor feeding, sweating and failure to thrive in infants
Recurrent chest infections with pulmonary overcirculation
Cyanosis, sometimes with hypercyanotic spells
Exertional breathlessness and reduced exercise capacity in older children and adults
Palpitations and syncope from arrhythmia
Many lesions are entirely asymptomatic and found on incidental examination
signs: Murmur — frequently the presenting finding
Central cyanosis and clubbing in right-to-left shunts
Fixed splitting of the second heart sound in atrial septal defect
Continuous machinery murmur in patent ductus arteriosus
Radiofemoral delay and upper limb hypertension in coarctation
Failure to thrive, tachypnoea and hepatomegaly in infants with heart failure

investigations.findings: The definitive anatomical and physiological assessment; fetal echocardiography allows planning of delivery and neonatal care.
Newborn screening that detects critical congenital heart disease before collapse.
Chamber enlargement patterns, axis deviation and pulmonary vascularity provide useful clues.
Essential in adults for complex anatomy, right ventricular volumes, shunt quantification and conduit assessment.
Haemodynamic assessment including pulmonary vascular resistance and shunt calculation, and a route for intervention.
Objective functional capacity, valuable for surveillance and timing of reintervention.

complications: Atrial and ventricular arrhythmia, particularly after surgical repair
Heart failure in the systemic ventricle
Complications of pregnancy in specific lesions
Need for reintervention and conduit replacement

treatment.principles: Management depends entirely on the specific lesion and its physiology. Many defects are repaired or palliated in childhood, but repair is rarely cure — lifelong specialist follow-up is the standard of care. Educational summary only; care must be delivered by specialist congenital heart disease services.

groups.name: Surgical repair and palliation
groups.detail: From simple defect closure to complex staged palliation such as the Fontan pathway for single ventricle physiology.

groups.name: Transcatheter intervention
groups.detail: Device closure of septal defects and ducts, balloon valvuloplasty, stenting of coarctation and transcatheter pulmonary valve implantation.

groups.name: Medical therapy
groups.detail: Diuretics and afterload reduction for heart failure, prostaglandin to maintain ductal patency in duct-dependent lesions, and pulmonary vasodilators in selected pulmonary hypertension.

groups.name: Arrhythmia management
groups.detail: Ablation and device therapy, taking account of altered anatomy and vascular access.

groups.name: Endocarditis prevention
groups.detail: Meticulous oral and skin hygiene, with antibiotic prophylaxis for defined high-risk lesions.

groups.name: Lifelong specialist follow-up
groups.detail: Structured transition from paediatric to adult congenital services, with pre-pregnancy counselling and contraception advice.

keyTakeaways: Congenital heart disease is the commonest congenital malformation.
Classify by physiology — shunt, obstruction or cyanosis — rather than memorising lesion lists.
Falling pulmonary vascular resistance after birth is why many shunts present weeks later.
Ventricular septal defect is the commonest lesion at birth; bicuspid aortic valve is the commonest overall.
Eisenmenger syndrome marks the point at which shunt closure becomes contraindicated.
Repair is not cure — adults with congenital heart disease need lifelong specialist follow-up.

name: Atrial Septal Defect
tagline: A communication between the atria causing left-to-right shunting, right heart volume overload, and the classic sign of fixed splitting of the second heart sound.
overview: An atrial septal defect is a persistent communication between the atria, allowing shunting driven by the difference in ventricular compliance rather than by a large pressure gradient. Secundum defects at the fossa ovalis are the commonest type; primum defects lie in the inferior septum and are part of the atrioventricular septal defect spectrum; sinus venosus defects sit near the caval orifices and are frequently associated with anomalous pulmonary venous drainage. A patent foramen ovale, present in roughly a quarter of adults, is not a true defect but a persistent flap valve, relevant chiefly to paradoxical embolism. Many defects go undetected into adulthood because the shunt is well tolerated for decades.

modifiable: Maternal exposures during early pregnancy, as for congenital heart disease generally
nonModifiable: Female sex, with a roughly 2:1 predominance for secundum defects
Holt–Oram syndrome and other familial syndromes
Family history of congenital heart disease

pathophysiology.title: Compliance-driven shunting
pathophysiology.text: The right ventricle is more compliant than the left, so during diastole the left atrium preferentially empties across the defect into the right atrium — a left-to-right shunt determined by relative ventricular compliance rather than by atrial pressures.

pathophysiology.title: Right heart volume overload
pathophysiology.text: The right atrium and ventricle receive both normal systemic venous return and the shunted volume, and progressively dilate.

pathophysiology.title: Increased pulmonary blood flow
pathophysiology.text: Pulmonary flow may be one and a half to three or more times systemic flow. This increased flow across normal pulmonary and tricuspid valves produces the characteristic flow murmurs.

pathophysiology.title: Fixed splitting of S2
pathophysiology.text: The large, relatively fixed right ventricular volume load prolongs right ventricular ejection throughout the respiratory cycle, so the normal inspiratory variation in splitting is abolished.

pathophysiology.title: Atrial remodelling and arrhythmia
pathophysiology.text: Chronic right atrial dilatation and stretch produce atrial fibrillation and flutter, typically appearing from the fourth decade onwards.

pathophysiology.title: Pulmonary vascular disease
pathophysiology.text: In a minority, sustained high pulmonary flow causes vascular remodelling with rising resistance, eventually leading to shunt reversal and Eisenmenger syndrome.

anatomyInvolved: Interatrial septum, particularly the fossa ovalis
Right atrium and right ventricle, both volume loaded
Tricuspid and pulmonary valves, carrying increased flow
Pulmonary arteries and pulmonary vascular bed
Pulmonary veins, in sinus venosus defects with anomalous drainage
physiologyChanges: Left-to-right shunt with pulmonary-to-systemic flow ratio above 1
Right atrial and right ventricular volume overload with dilatation
Increased flow across the pulmonary and tricuspid valves
Paradoxical septal motion from right ventricular volume loading
Potential for paradoxical embolism when right atrial pressure transiently exceeds left

progression.text: Usually asymptomatic; often detected because of an incidental murmur. Small secundum defects may close spontaneously.
Exercise intolerance may be present but is frequently unrecognised, having developed gradually.
Atrial arrhythmias, progressive right heart dilatation and reduced exercise capacity become apparent.
Pulmonary hypertension, right heart failure and, in a minority, shunt reversal with Eisenmenger physiology.

symptoms: Frequently asymptomatic for decades
Exertional breathlessness and fatigue
Palpitations from atrial arrhythmia
Recurrent chest infections in children with large shunts
Stroke or transient ischaemic attack from paradoxical embolism
signs: Wide and fixed splitting of the second heart sound — the cardinal sign
Ejection systolic murmur at the upper left sternal edge from increased pulmonary flow
Tricuspid mid-diastolic flow murmur at the lower left sternal edge with large shunts
Left parasternal heave from right ventricular volume overload
Raised JVP and signs of right heart failure in advanced disease
Cyanosis and clubbing only once the shunt has reversed

investigations.findings: Defect location and size, direction of shunting, right heart dilatation, paradoxical septal motion and estimated pulmonary pressures.
Bubbles crossing to the left side within a few cardiac cycles confirm an interatrial communication.
Defines defect margins and rims, essential for assessing suitability for device closure, and identifies sinus venosus defects.
Quantifies shunt fraction and right ventricular volumes, and identifies anomalous pulmonary venous drainage.
Right axis deviation with incomplete right bundle branch block in secundum defects; left axis deviation in primum defects — a useful discriminator.
Oximetry step-up quantifies the shunt; pulmonary vascular resistance determines whether closure is safe.

complications: Device- or surgery-related complications including residual shunt and erosion

treatment.principles: Closure is indicated for haemodynamically significant defects with right heart volume overload, provided pulmonary vascular resistance has not risen prohibitively. Closure improves symptoms and right ventricular size at any age, though arrhythmia risk persists if closure is late. Educational summary only.

groups.name: Observation
groups.detail: Small defects without right heart dilatation may simply be monitored.

groups.name: Transcatheter device closure
groups.detail: The treatment of choice for secundum defects with adequate rims.

groups.name: Surgical closure
groups.detail: Required for primum and sinus venosus defects, for very large defects, and where pulmonary venous drainage must be rerouted.

groups.name: Arrhythmia management
groups.detail: Rhythm or rate control with anticoagulation; concomitant surgical ablation may be considered.

groups.name: Pulmonary hypertension assessment
groups.detail: Careful haemodynamic evaluation before closure; closure is contraindicated once the shunt has reversed.

keyTakeaways: Shunting is driven by relative ventricular compliance, not by a large atrial pressure difference.
Wide fixed splitting of the second heart sound is the cardinal clinical sign.
Murmurs arise from increased flow across normal valves, not from the defect itself.
Secundum defects show right axis deviation; primum defects show left axis deviation.
Presentation is often delayed to adulthood with arrhythmia or exercise intolerance.
A patent foramen ovale is a flap valve, not a true septal defect.

name: Hypertension
tagline: Sustained elevation of arterial pressure — largely asymptomatic, the leading modifiable cardiovascular risk factor, and a driver of almost every other cardiac disease.
overview: Hypertension is sustained elevation of arterial blood pressure above thresholds at which treatment reduces cardiovascular events. Roughly 90–95% of cases are primary (essential), arising from a complex interaction of genetic susceptibility, sodium handling, sympathetic and renin–angiotensin activity, vascular stiffness and lifestyle. The remainder are secondary to identifiable causes such as renal disease, renal artery stenosis, primary aldosteronism, phaeochromocytoma, Cushing's syndrome, coarctation, obstructive sleep apnoea or drugs. It is overwhelmingly asymptomatic, which is why it has been called the silent killer, and its consequences are delivered through target organ damage in the heart, brain, kidneys, retina and arteries. Diagnostic thresholds differ between major guidelines, so always state which definition is being used.

modifiable: High dietary sodium and low potassium intake
NSAIDs, corticosteroids, combined oral contraceptives, decongestants and stimulants
nonModifiable: Ethnicity, with higher prevalence and earlier onset in some populations

pathophysiology.title: Determinants of pressure
pathophysiology.text: Mean arterial pressure is the product of cardiac output and systemic vascular resistance. In established primary hypertension the dominant abnormality is raised systemic vascular resistance with a normal cardiac output.

pathophysiology.title: Sodium and volume handling
pathophysiology.text: A rightward shift in the renal pressure–natriuresis relationship means the kidney requires a higher perfusion pressure to excrete a given sodium load, resetting pressure upward.

pathophysiology.title: Neurohormonal activation
pathophysiology.text: Increased sympathetic outflow and inappropriate activation of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system raise vascular tone and promote sodium retention and vascular remodelling.

pathophysiology.title: Endothelial dysfunction
pathophysiology.text: Reduced nitric oxide bioavailability and increased endothelin and oxidative stress shift the vascular balance towards vasoconstriction.

pathophysiology.title: Vascular remodelling
pathophysiology.text: Arterioles undergo hypertrophic and eutrophic remodelling with an increased wall-to-lumen ratio, raising resistance further and creating a self-perpetuating cycle.

pathophysiology.title: Large artery stiffening
pathophysiology.text: Elastin fragmentation and collagen deposition reduce aortic compliance, raising systolic and pulse pressure — the mechanism of isolated systolic hypertension in older people.

pathophysiology.title: Cardiac consequences
pathophysiology.text: Chronic pressure loading produces concentric left ventricular hypertrophy with impaired relaxation, reduced coronary flow reserve, atrial dilatation and an increased risk of arrhythmia and heart failure.

anatomyInvolved: Systemic arterioles — the resistance vessels
Large elastic arteries, which stiffen over time
Left ventricle, which hypertrophies concentrically
Kidneys, both cause and victim of hypertension
Retinal arterioles, where damage is directly visible
Cerebral vasculature
physiologyChanges: Increased systemic vascular resistance with normal cardiac output in established disease
Rightward shift of the renal pressure–natriuresis curve
Concentric left ventricular hypertrophy with diastolic dysfunction
Reduced arterial compliance with widened pulse pressure
Impaired cerebral and renal autoregulation, shifted to higher pressures
Reduced coronary flow reserve despite normal epicardial arteries

progression.text: Raised readings with no detectable target organ involvement. Lifestyle intervention is the priority.
Left ventricular hypertrophy, albuminuria, retinopathy or increased arterial stiffness appear, still without symptoms.
Coronary disease, heart failure, stroke, chronic kidney disease or peripheral arterial disease develop.
Severe elevation with acute target organ damage — encephalopathy, aortic dissection, acute heart failure, acute kidney injury or retinal haemorrhage — requiring immediate, controlled reduction.

symptoms: Asymptomatic in the great majority — this is the defining clinical feature
Headache, usually only with severe elevation
Symptoms of a secondary cause: episodic headache, palpitations and sweating in phaeochromocytoma; muscle weakness in primary aldosteronism
Symptoms of target organ damage: chest pain, breathlessness, visual disturbance, neurological deficit
signs: Elevated blood pressure on repeated, properly performed measurement — correct cuff size and technique matter
Sustained, non-displaced apex beat and a fourth heart sound with left ventricular hypertrophy
Hypertensive retinopathy on fundoscopy, graded by severity
Radiofemoral delay in coarctation; renal bruits in renal artery stenosis
Features of Cushing's syndrome or thyroid disease where relevant

investigations.modality: Ambulatory or home blood pressure monitoring
investigations.findings: Confirms the diagnosis and identifies white-coat and masked hypertension; better correlated with outcome than clinic readings.
Renal function, electrolytes, glucose, HbA1c, lipids and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio to assess damage and screen for causes.
Left ventricular hypertrophy, strain pattern, left atrial abnormality or atrial fibrillation.
Left ventricular mass, wall thickness, diastolic function and left atrial volume, where the ECG or clinical picture warrants it.
Direct visualisation of arteriolar narrowing, arteriovenous nipping, haemorrhages, exudates and papilloedema.
Aldosterone-to-renin ratio, plasma or urinary metanephrines, renal imaging and sleep studies, guided by clinical suspicion — particularly in young or resistant hypertension.

complications: Coronary artery disease and myocardial infarction
Heart failure, particularly with preserved ejection fraction
Chronic kidney disease and end-stage renal failure

treatment.principles: Treatment aims to reduce cardiovascular events, not simply to normalise a number. Lifestyle modification underpins all management. Drug choice considers age, ethnicity, comorbidity and the presence of target organ damage, and combination therapy — often as a single-pill combination — is usually required to reach target. Educational summary only; thresholds and targets differ between guidelines and must be applied from current recommendations.

groups.name: Lifestyle modification
groups.detail: Sodium reduction, DASH-style diet, weight loss, regular aerobic activity, alcohol moderation and smoking cessation.

groups.name: Renin–angiotensin system inhibitors
groups.detail: ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers, particularly valuable with diabetes, albuminuria or heart failure.

groups.name: Calcium channel blockers
groups.detail: Dihydropyridines, often first-line in older patients and in some ethnic groups.

groups.name: Thiazide-like diuretics
groups.detail: Effective, well-studied, and useful in combination therapy.

groups.name: Additional agents
groups.detail: Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists for resistant hypertension, plus beta-blockers and alpha-blockers where there is a specific indication.

groups.name: Treating secondary causes
groups.detail: Adrenalectomy or targeted therapy for aldosteronism, renal artery intervention in selected cases, CPAP for sleep apnoea.

groups.name: Adherence support
groups.detail: Single-pill combinations, home monitoring and structured follow-up — adherence is a principal determinant of control.

keyTakeaways: Mean arterial pressure = cardiac output × systemic vascular resistance; raised resistance dominates in established disease.
Around 90–95% of hypertension is primary; screen for secondary causes in young, severe or resistant cases.
It is asymptomatic — the diagnosis is made by measurement, not by symptoms.
Out-of-office measurement correlates better with outcomes than clinic readings.
Isolated systolic hypertension in older adults reflects large artery stiffening.
Target organ damage — left ventricular hypertrophy, albuminuria, retinopathy — refines risk and guides urgency.
Diagnostic thresholds differ between guidelines; always state which you are applying.
